title: Mansa Musa's Hajj
hook: Mali's king travels to Mecca with so much gold that Cairo's prices fall

segments.voice: Yesterday, the empire of Mali, with safe roads and a dead stranger's goods kept for his heir. Your line was: the empire of Mali. Did you give back something that wasn't yours? Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

Cairo, the palace of the sultan of Egypt. A visiting king from West Africa is brought in, and the courtiers tell him what everyone does here: kiss the ground before the sultan. He refuses. He has come as a pilgrim, on his way to Mecca, and he won't bow to a man. The room goes tense. Then someone beside him whispers a word, and the visitor speaks: he bows, he says, to God who created him. And he goes down in prostration. The sultan lets it pass, and treats him with honor. The Cairo writer al-Umari heard the story from people who were there. Today: Mansa Musa's Hajj.
screen: `A KING AT THE SULTAN'S COURT.` → `HE WON'T BOW TO A MAN.` → `I BOW TO GOD WHO CREATED ME.`

segments.voice: Hajj is not optional for a Muslim who can manage it. In Pickthall's translation of the Qur'an: "And pilgrimage to the House is a duty unto Allah for mankind, for him who can find a way thither." Mansa Musa, king of Mali, could find a way. He crossed the desert with a great company of people and a great deal of gold, and he did not keep it to himself. In Cairo he spent and gave so freely, al-Umari reports, that gold lost its value in the city, and the people of Cairo were still talking about it years later. Turn that around for a moment. A man gave away so much that the price of the thing he gave fell. And then there is the ending. On the way home, al-Umari says, Mansa Musa ran short, and had to borrow from the merchants of Cairo. The king of gold, in debt at the end of his pilgrimage. Some people call him the richest pilgrim. Nobody can really count his gold. What the sources describe is something else: a pilgrim who refused to bow to a sultan, bowed to God instead, gave without counting, and came home with less. After the Hajj, tradition says, Mali's name traveled north to the cities of the Mediterranean, and scholars and builders traveled back with him. Generosity, here, was not a side detail. It was the story.
screen: `A DUTY FOR WHOEVER CAN FIND A WAY.` · `SO MUCH GOLD THAT ITS VALUE FELL.` · `THE KING BORROWS TO GET HOME.` · `MALI'S NAME TRAVELS NORTH.` · then, large: `THE RICHEST PILGRIM.`

segments.voice: The practice: give generously. Settle, and breathe. Generosity doesn't need gold. It needs something you would rather keep. Your time, your attention, money, praise, the last of something good. Let one person come to mind who could use what you have. Notice what in you hesitates, and don't argue with it; just see it. Then decide on one gift for today, slightly bigger than feels comfortable. If you pray, you can offer that gift to God before you give it. If you don't, simply hold the person in mind. The bell holds the time.
Mansa Musa's Hajj. The king of Mali's pilgrimage to Mecca, when he gave so much in Cairo that gold lost its value there. Today's word.
Your line: the richest pilgrim. Today, give one gift, of time or money or care, a little larger than you'd planned. Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims who are able are called to make the Hajj to Mecca, and the Qur'an's call to spend in charity travels with them. In West Africa, Mansa Musa's pilgrimage is still told as part of Mali's history.
